voiceover: If you and your friend both use "password123," without a salt you'd get the exact same hash. That's a problem. Attackers precompute hashes for millions of common passwords, then just look up stolen hashes in a table. Instant match. The fix is a salt: a random string the site mixes into your password before hashing, unique for every user. It's stored right next to the hash. It isn't secret; it just makes every hash different, so those precomputed tables become useless. Good sites also use deliberately slow hashes, so every single guess costs time. Salt can't save a weak password, though. Part three: how a site remembers it's you.
